note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

precepts.why:
Samuel asked Saul, “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?” King Saul had an issue with being obedient to the Lord, and God called that disobedience evil in his sight. Saul answered, “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord”, and then, “But the people took of the spoil.” Was that a sign of godly sorrow? No, there was none involved. Isaiah 58:9 names what Saul was doing.

“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity.”

What is the putting forth of the finger? That is blaming. Saul blamed the people right after saying he had kept Agag alive. He blamed the people for keeping the sheep and the best of the flocks, but did not take accountability for keeping Agag the Amalekite alive. So what does the Lord say? He is not going to hear any of us until we stop playing the blame game. The Lord answers, “Here I am”, when the finger is taken away.

Stop blaming others. How are you dealing with that situation? I am bitter against this person because they did this to me; I have hatred towards this person because of this. The Lord does not care about your reasoning or your justification, because every one of us will be judged according to our ways. The Lord sees how that person is treating you, and the same way he sees how you are reacting to that treatment. If you trust in the Lord, you act according to how God commanded you to deal with that situation, and then let the Lord deal with that person.

That is a building block of bitterness. Disobedience, then justifying yourself, then blaming others: the bitterness is compounded on sins that were already there. As 1 Samuel 15:22 says, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.”

This is the wisdom Samuel applied, and the wisdom we have to learn to apply: “Never trust thine enemy: for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness.”

“Though he humble himself, and go crouching”: is that not exactly what Agag did, coming delicately? “Yet take good heed and beware of him, and thou shalt be unto him as if thou hadst wiped a lookingglass, and thou shalt know that his rust hath not been altogether wiped away.”

The things that were written aforetime were written for our learning. Esau does not forget, but we do, because we are not tapped into the scriptures. When we apply what the scriptures show us, we learn that our enemies have been the same from day one, and they are not going to change. That is the perpetual hatred we never learned.

note.label: The Bold and the Bashful

precepts.why:
What is going on in 1 Samuel 15? The Lord commanded Saul to utterly destroy all the Amalekites and everything they have, every last one of them. The Lord told Saul, wipe these devils out. And he didn’t do it.

The commandment was total: “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” All that they have. All means everything.

Now hold that against Saul’s answer in verse 20: “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.” Wait a minute: the king is still alive. What do you mean you followed the commandment of the Lord? Saul is playing the defensive, justifying himself, making excuses.

Then verse 21: “But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.” It wasn’t me, it was the people, it was their fault; I couldn’t do nothing about it. That is bashfulness: you don’t take accountability. The commandment said spare the sheep and oxen not, and Saul brought them back and blamed the people.

So Samuel answered, “to obey is better than sacrifice.” To do what you were told is better than coming back saying, my bad, I thought I understood what you wanted, I decided to do it this way. You fulfill the commandment you were given, and if there is a problem, you say something.

precepts.why:
Saul finally confessed in verse 24: “I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” If you are a leader and you are in fear of your people, or you don’t want them to be mad at you, what can those people do to you? Manipulate you. You are a pushover; they can sway you to the left and to the right. Who is supposed to move you? The Lord, not the people you are supposed to lead. You are not leading the people; you are being led by the people.

Then verse 28: “And Samuel said unto him, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” Damn.

That is what the bashful spirit costs. Verse 23 already said it: “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.” When you are in that spirit the Lord can’t use you; you are not a good leader. Leadership may see something in you and put you in a position, and then when we question you on certain things you make excuses, or you separate yourself into a bubble with the men under you. You are bashful, you are bringing up a bunch of bashful brothers under you, and you are keeping the brothers under you hostage.

The Lord had made Saul king “When thou wast little in thine own sight”, when he thought he was a nobody. And because he feared the people and would not obey, the kingdom was torn from him and given to his neighbour, David, who was better than he.

precepts.point: Thou desirest not sacrifice, thou delightest not in burnt offering; the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit and a contrite heart. The animals were temporary; a broken and humbled mind is the sacrifice he wants, and only then are the bullocks on the altar acceptable.

note.label: The Mercy and Humility of King Manasseh

precepts.why:
Psalms 51:16: “For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.” David is saying, you don’t desire sacrifice, otherwise I would give it to you; you don’t care about that either. The Lord revealed to David, I don’t care about sacrifices. And Saul didn’t listen either.

“And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Samuel is asking the question: does the Lord require sacrifices above obeying what he tells you to do?

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” To hearken is to listen and humble yourself. That is better than the fat of rams.

So “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” The sacrifice God accepts is a broken spirit. The animals were just temporary; your mind being broken and humbled is the best sacrifice the Lord desires. You can offer and sacrifice all you want, but make sure you offer with a good heart. “Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.” Once the sacrifices of righteousness are offered, then the bullocks on the altar become acceptable.

precepts.text: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings as in obeying his voice? To obey is better than sacrifice, as Saul learned.
precepts.point: Whosoever shall keep the whole law and yet offend in one point is guilty of all: the Christian says you cannot keep them, but the context is the royal law, as the next verse shows, he that said do not commit adultery said also do not kill. Speak and do as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty, since Christ redeemed us from the death the moral law carried; he shall have judgment without mercy that hath showed no mercy.

precepts.why:
Saul disobeyed a direct order, and through Samuel the Lord asks him a question: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Answer it.

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” The Lord cared about obedience more than animal sacrifices.

That is the same point as Mark 12:33, that loving God and your neighbour “is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Saul wanted to bring the sacrifice after he had disobeyed; Israel wanted to bring the best animal after they had wronged their neighbour. The Lord wants the obedience. And that is why James 2 holds us to the royal law, love thy neighbour as thyself, and not to an offering that covers over a sin against the brother.

precepts.text: Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Stubbornness is satanic worship.
precepts.point: If you cannot uphold righteousness when nobody is looking, that is your future: damnation, judgment, destruction. Stubborn goes back to bullheaded, and bullheaded goes back to Baal.

note.label: The Iranians & The Ephesians

precepts.why:
Judges 2:19 ends: “they ceased not from their own doings, nor from their stubborn way.” Stubborn goes back to bullheaded, and bullheaded goes back to Baal. 1 Samuel 15:23 says what stubbornness really is.

“For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” Bullheaded, stubborn, is idolatry. It is satanic worship.

That is how Israel gets down: “when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers.” Whenever there is not a judge, a leader, in place, they go to their lonesome. They get relaxed: the officer is not here, the captain is not here, the deacon is not here, the bishop ain’t here, let’s go back to our lonesome. If that is your spirit, you are going to get the same judgment. If you can’t uphold righteousness when nobody is looking, that is your future: damnation, judgment, destruction.

Ecclesiasticus 30:12, read just before, gives the remedy: “Bow down his neck while he is young, and beat him on the sides while he is a child, lest he wax stubborn.” That is why God’s laws are taught without going to the left or to the right, and without playing games. We know how we got over here: through stubbornness. So if we want to get delivered, we have to wake the hell up.

note.label: Exodus 17: Water Out of the Rock and War With Amalek

precepts.why:
“the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.” Hundreds of years after Moses, the Lord sent Saul by Samuel to keep that oath: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.”

The Lord remembered what Amalek did coming out of Egypt, and the Amalekites of Saul's day, who had not been there, were to be utterly destroyed for it, man and woman, infant and suckling. God be true and every man a liar: the nations do not get away with what they did to His people, and the judgment carries to the seed.

Saul did not finish Agag's line, and in Esther's day Haman the Agagite, of that same seed, rose against Israel. The war truly runs from generation to generation.

precepts.text: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have.

note.label: Deuteronomy 25: Just Judgment, the Brother's Duty, and Amalek

precepts.why:
“Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt”, and blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.”

The Lord remembered what Amalek did, laying wait in the way when Israel came up from Egypt and smiting the hindmost, the feeble, the faint and weary. Once Israel had rest from their enemies round about, the remembrance of Amalek was to be blotted out, and here is the command to do it: utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not.

precepts.point: It takes strength to observe to do according to all the law; that is why the scriptures speak of building up your faith and being exercised in the things you learn. You have to be spiritually fit to survive in this truth, especially as a leader. The word for being strong and very courageous is fortitude, one of the virtues that comes with wisdom.

note.label: Joshua 1: The Charge to Joshua and the Formula for Success

precepts.why:
“turn not from it to the right hand or to the left” means no deviating from the word and no hunting loopholes. Saul is the example. He was told to spare nothing, yet “Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.”

He spared Agag and the best of the animals, and it cost him the kingdom. That is turning to the right hand or to the left. Joshua was to observe to do according to all the law, “that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest”; Saul deviated from it and lost everything.

The Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness. That answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers.

Then he warned the Kenites: “Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt.”

“And the children of the Kenite, Moses’ father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah”. note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
“It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments.” Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you.

“And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the Lord all night.” Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost: “The beginning of pride is when one departeth from God, and his heart is turned away from his Maker. For pride is the beginning of sin, and he that hath it shall pour out abomination: and therefore the Lord brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly. The Lord hath cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.”

That is exactly what happened. Saul’s heart turned from his Maker, he poured out sin upon sin from there, and the Lord cast down the proud prince’s throne and set up the meek in his stead. That is the whole story that follows.

precepts.text: What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it; the Most High made a law for the bright ideas that come along the way of following instructions, and it is plain.
precepts.point: Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul “came to Carmel, and, behold, he set him up a place”, a monument to himself. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name. Do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more.

The first thing out of Saul’s mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed: “Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord.” Samuel answers, “What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear?” If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals?

Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: “They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.” Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

precepts.point: And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in Deuteronomy 25. Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
“When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel?” Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance.

That is how Saul started. He had answered Samuel, “Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?” That was the little-in-his-own-sight attitude: he thought nothing of himself, with no confidence to be a ruler, and the Most High still chose him.

Then the Lord sent him on the errand of the vengeance written in Deuteronomy 25: “Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed.” “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?” Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

precepts.text: If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me; when you plead your own righteousness against correction, you end up revealing more of your rebellion out of your own mouth, which is exactly what Saul did.
precepts.point: In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
Saul is in denial: “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me”. Samuel breaks down the rebuke, and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong.

In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion. He “brought Agag the king of Amalek”, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted. Then he lays the spoil on the people again: “the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed”.

“If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me: if I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse.” When you plead your own righteousness against correction, you end up revealing more of your rebellion out of your own mouth, which is exactly what Saul did.

precepts.text: Obstinate is another word for stubborn: the mind set on doing what it wants contrary to counsel will be laden with sorrows, and Saul heaped sin upon sin, lying, justifying himself, and blaming the people, which is what carried him into the witchcraft and idolatry of rebellion.
precepts.point: This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
“For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft.

Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king”: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in.

“A stubborn heart shall fare evil at the last; and he that loveth danger shall perish therein. An obstinate heart shall be laden with sorrows; and the wicked man shall heap sin upon sin.” Obstinate is another word for stubborn: the mind set on doing what it wants contrary to counsel will be laden with sorrows. Saul heaped sin upon sin, lying, justifying himself and blaming the people, and that is what carried him into the witchcraft and idolatry of rebellion.

This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last. Saul’s end comes in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Then he asks, “pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord”: take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

“The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the Lord shall be safe.” If you fear what the people will say, you will fall into the trap and transgress. That is why a leader cannot fold when the people become too much to handle. Saul would have been safe had he trusted the Lord.

precepts.text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it?
precepts.point: And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

note.label: 1 Samuel 15: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice

precepts.why:
As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul “laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.” Samuel said, “The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him. Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13.

“And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.” “God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?” What he said over Saul, he will do.

The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan. If a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Saul laid hold of the prophet’s mantle, but the sentence on Saul stood: “the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent”.

precepts.text: Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft; the road Saul took after the spirit departed ends with him literally at witchcraft.
precepts.point: Chapter 15 said rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and Saul is now headed down that downward spiral; the spirit is leaving him, and he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” Simultaneously, as the Most High put his spirit on David, the spirit departed from Saul. Note it well: the evil spirit came from the Lord. That is a teaching the church world leaves out.

Chapter 15 said, “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” Saul is now headed down that downward spiral. The spirit is leaving him, and the road Saul took ends with him literally at witchcraft: he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

precepts.text: Saul was told to overcome nations and did not, and was told not to go to his last battle yet went and died there; obedience is better than sacrifice.
precepts.point: David did exactly as commanded and smote them from Gibeon to Gazer. The lesson is precise obedience: if he says do not go up, do not go up; if he says go this way, do not go that way.

note.label: 1 Chronicles 14: David Established and Inquiring of the Most High

precepts.why:
“Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.”

Saul was told to overcome nations and did not. He was told not to go to his last battle, yet he went and died there. “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.”

David is the other side of it: “David therefore did as God commanded him: and they smote the host of the Philistines from Gibeon even to Gazer.” The lesson is precise obedience. If he says do not go up, do not go up; if he says go this way, do not go that way.

precepts.text: Saul spared Agag king of the Amalekites when he was commanded to utterly destroy them, so the Agagite line lived on and Haman descends from Amalek, which explains his deep disdain for Israel.
precepts.point: The servants asked daily why Mordecai transgressed the king's commandment, and he hearkened not, but told them he was a Jew, and they told Haman to see whether Mordecai's matter would stand. We do not bow, the same as the three Hebrew children did not bow to the image in Babylon, for we pledge allegiance to none but the Most High.

note.label: Esther 3: Haman the Agagite and the Decree to Destroy the Jews

precepts.why:
Haman is “the son of Hammedatha the Agagite”, and that name reaches back to Saul. Saul told Samuel, “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.” He had been commanded to utterly destroy them, and he says he did, but he brought Agag the king of Amalek back alive. He spared him.

Because Saul spared Agag, the Agagite line lived on, and Haman is of it: he descends from Amalek. That explains his deep disdain for Israel. When the king set his seat above all the princes and commanded that all bow, an Amalekite was set over the king's gate, and Mordecai the Jew bowed not.

precepts.text: Agag was king of the Amalekites, taken alive by Saul, which is the stock the Agagite Aman comes from.
precepts.point: The teaching traces who Aman was. He is the same Aman promoted in the canonical book, an Agagite, and the Agagites descend from Agag king of the Amalekites, and Amalek descends from Esau. This is the lineage that has warred against Israel throughout history and has always been unsuccessful, for the Most High delivered his people.

note.label: Esther 12: Mardocheus Uncovers the Plot and Aman's Hatred

precepts.why:
Aman is called “the Agagite”, and Agag is a name with a history. Saul “took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.” Agag was king of the Amalekites; the Agagites descend from him, and that is the stock Aman comes from.

So when Aman sought to molest Mardocheus and his people, it was an Amalekite rising against Israel again. That line warred against Israel throughout history and was always unsuccessful, for the Most High delivered his people.

precepts.text: The Lord delights in obeying his voice more than in burnt offerings and sacrifices; to obey is better than sacrifice and to hearken than the fat of rams.
precepts.point: Even in David's time he understood that sacrifice and offering were not what the Lord desired. There are multiple places where the Lord was not looking for the sacrifices.

note.label: Psalm 40: Patient Waiting, Obedience Over Sacrifice, and the Great Congregation

precepts.why:
“Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.” Even in David's time he understood that sacrifice and offering were not what the Lord desired. Samuel said the same: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.”

There are multiple places where the Lord was not looking for the sacrifices. Sacrifice is really just a show of your obedience; obeying his voice is what he delights in. “mine ears hast thou opened”: the opened ear that hearkens is worth more than the fat of rams.

precepts.text: To obey is better than sacrifice; the Most High delights in obeying his voice more than burnt offerings.
precepts.point: For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David.

precepts.why:
“For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.” Samuel said the same to Saul: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” The Most High delights in obeying his voice more than in burnt offerings.

David knew that, and Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David. To obey is better than sacrifice.

Because sometimes we will say, oh, for the multitude of my oblations the Lord is not going to remember my sins. For the multitude of my sacrifices the Lord is not going to remember my sins. points: And Samuel said unto him, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. So now I want to paint the picture. Saul is dealing with rebellion. Saul is dealing with disobedience. Saul is dealing with rejecting the Lord, putting forth the finger, playing the blame game. Now the Lord told the prophet Samuel, hey, let him know that I am choosing one of his neighbours, and someone that is better than him.

Do you see how bitterness can start to build? I want you to see the progression, or the building blocks, of bitterness. There are other contributing factors first. Now I am going to give you an example. You get removed from an office. Now someone else is put into that same office. Now you start looking at that person with an evil eye, as though they took your job. Is that not how it goes? So I am the only one that sees that?

But it is a progression, because there was something already there. That is the point. There are things that you build upon, and then at the top of it all you have that bitterness. Then the hatred will evolve. Then it turns to malice and violence.

And I am not just projecting these words out there. I am meditating on these words as well. Because even as I am reading this this morning and last night, I am like, let me pay closer attention to this portion or to that portion, because the word of God is quick and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword, and it is the discerner of the thoughts and intents of men. So I have got to make sure that I am not rejecting the word of God, and I am not playing the blame game either.

And hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. That is better than King Saul. That had to sit in the back of his mind, because at the time that neighbour was not risen up yet. So now he is looking like, who is it? Now you start looking at everybody. This is for you brothers that think or make these claims that all leadership hates you. All of them. Everybody. This is when that bitterness creeps in and you are trying to find who to place the full blame on. So instead of having one person, you just blanket the whole statement. The camp knows who I am talking to, because there are a couple of them in this region, and these brothers are like, the whole congregation hates me, everyone on the sister side hates me, all the brothers hate me, they do not want me to succeed. Right now Satan is all in your mind and in your ear.

That is the argument you hear today: that was not me; I never held anyone in slavery. But the Lord said destroy them for what their forefathers did in Exodus. The nations pay for the sins of their fathers, the same way we are paying for the sins of ours: our fathers refused God's commandments, the curses fell on them and their seed, and here we are generations of oppression later. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows Leviticus 19:18 applies to the children of thy people.

Understand the frame: we live peaceably with all men and lay hands on no one; we do not incite or condone any violence, and if we hear of any we report it. The day of Psalms 137 has not yet come; it belongs to the return of the Lord, so chill out and relax, none of that is for now.

A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft.

Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross.
Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in.

This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.
